thread.title: Purdue holds election forum, explains rules on registration - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: Purdue holds election forum, explains rules on registration - NewsBreak

author: ROBERT LANGEN Staff Reporter
title: Purdue holds election forum, explains rules on registration - NewsBreak
text:
By ROBERT LANGEN Staff Reporter ,
5 hours ago Several members of the community marched to the CoRec to encourage students to vote. The group marched from the Purdue Memorial Union to the CoRec in 2024. Exponent File Photo Purdue administrators and the Tippecanoe County Board of Elections and Registration held a meeting, explaining voting guidelines regarding campus clubs and countywide voting ahead of the May 5 primary.
During the event the panel, which included Senior Vice President and General Counsel Steven Schultz, Professor of Teaching Gina DelSanto, and Assistant Director for Civics Literacy Fred Duttlinger, explained Purdue wants to move responsibility of promoting students to vote to the clubs.
“As an institution, we’ve decided to focus our efforts by supporting student organizations themselves,” the panel said.
Officials told campus leaders that student groups can help expand voter participation, but voter registration efforts must remain strictly nonpartisan and follow university policies.
Schultz, Purdue’s top lawyer, framed the discussion of voter registration around three principles Purdue stakeholders should keep in mind: efforts must be nonpartisan, comply with campus policies, and be done correctly so students who believe they registered are not turned away later.
Purdue has an institutional neutrality policy, and Schultz said the university is a venue for debate, rather than an institution that takes sides in contested political issues. Purdue’s approach is to support free expression while maintaining reasonable time, place, and manner regulations, including when organizations reserve space for canvassing or registration, Schultz said.
For student groups planning registration drives, Mike Smith, a staff member of the Tippecanoe County Board of Elections and Registration for over 42 years, encouraged using the state voter registration form. He said it allows the registrant to receive a receipt and identifies the person accepting the form, which can help election officials resolve problems if a registration is missing or unclear.
The panel gave guidelines on how clubs should distribute candidate literature. If a club wants to have a voter-registration event, it has to be strictly nonpartisan.
University staff said the key distinction between registration and promoting a candidate is that while registration is nonpartisan, candidate promotion is partisan. The practical advice, they said, is to separate the activities into two events, so voter registration events are clearly nonpartisan.
Staff also said funding decisions follow the same line. A nonpartisan event, such as voter access, voter information, or transportation support, may be eligible to apply for university funding through student organization channels. But, candidate advocacy would have to come from a group’s own funds.
Smith added a legal warning for groups that conduct registration drives in any context. If a group is registering voters, it cannot selectively assist only supporters of one party or candidate.
“If you’re conducting voter registration, you have to accept anybody who comes up and assist anybody,” Smith said.
Student voting
Smith walked attendees through election administration basics and common pitfalls for student voters. Smith said Indiana requires voters to be registered at least 29 days before an election and said voters can only be registered in one place at a time.
Smith also urged out-of-state students to weigh the potential consequences of registering in Indiana, saying his office has seen cases where students’ home states treated Indiana registration as a residency change, which affected state-based financial aid.
On voting access, Smith said Tippecanoe County operates as a vote center county, meaning registered county voters can vote at any vote center location in the county, rather than a single assigned precinct site.
Indiana requires a qualifying photo ID. Student IDs are currently not accepted under S.B. 10, but the law is currently under legal challenge.
Resources for student groups
Later discussion turned to resources for student groups. The discussion was led by Purdue Student Government Pro-Tempore Olivia Williams and Student Vice President Nicholas Neuman.
University staff said registration materials can be provided through the county at no cost, and that reserving space for a drive generally does not require payment.
The student government discussed concerns about poll accessibility. Williams said the First United Methodist Church, one of the polling stations Purdue said it would have for students, is not within walking distance from campus.
In response, DelSanto said the CoRec is very accessible to students, and there is a bus for students to use. The CoRec is located at 355 N. Martin Jischke Dr.
